summary: Compare REST, GraphQL, and RPC: three ways for programs to request data and actions.
goals: How REST resources and HTTP verbs work
How GraphQL requests only selected fields
How services use RPC to call each other
How to page through lists and change APIs safely

steps.title: Programs need an agreement
body: A mobile app shows a profile with a name, avatar, recent posts, and follower count. That data is on the server, so the app needs a way to request it. An API is the agreed contract: which addresses exist, what the app sends, and what the server returns. Here the app sends JSON over HTTPS.
steps.callout: An API is a promise to its users. Once apps depend on it, changes must avoid breaking them.

steps.title: REST: resources and HTTP actions
body: REST organizes data as resources with addresses, such as /users/42 or /users/42/posts. HTTP verbs say what to do: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH updates, and DELETE removes. This style is simple and works with many tools. Browsers and CDNs can cache many GET responses. GET, PUT, and DELETE are usually idempotent: repeating them has the same result as doing them once. POST may create another item each time, which matters when retrying.
steps.callout: HTTP status codes describe the result: 200 OK, 201 Created, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests, or 500 server error.

steps.title: Too many calls and too much data
body: On a phone, each network round trip may take about 100 ms. The app makes three requests one after another. Some requests may need an ID from an earlier response, so they cannot run at the same time. Each API response also returns a whole object: 48 KB arrive even though the screen needs about 3 KB. This is over-fetching. Needing several requests to get the data for one screen is under-fetching.
steps.callout: Extra round trips and unused data hurt most on slow networks, which is common for mobile users.

steps.title: GraphQL asks for selected fields
body: With GraphQL, the app sends one query describing the fields it wants. A GraphQL server fetches those fields from the services behind it and returns them in one response. In the diagram, one request goes from the phone, splits between Users and Posts services, then returns as one response.
steps.callout: GraphQL can help when iOS, Android, web, or TV clients need different fields from the same backend.

steps.title: Flexible queries need limits
body: Clients can ask for any data allowed by the schema, including followers of followers and all of their posts. A deeply nested request can overload the Users service. GraphQL queries are often sent as POST requests to one URL, so ordinary HTTP caches and CDNs cannot cache them without extra work, such as persisted queries.
steps.callout: Production GraphQL APIs should limit query depth and cost. They may also allow only approved, or “persisted,” queries.

steps.title: Call internal services with RPC
body: Services inside a data center often call one another using RPC (remote procedure call). The caller invokes a function on another machine, much like calling a local function. A common option is gRPC. Both sides use a typed schema, often Protocol Buffers, and generated code. The messages are compact binary data sent over HTTP/2.
steps.callout: gRPC is fast, typed, and supports streaming. Browsers usually need a gRPC-Web proxy, so it is more common between internal services.

steps.title: Split a long list into pages
body: A celebrity may have two million followers. Returning the whole list would take hundreds of megabytes and a long time. APIs split long lists into pages. An offset request such as ?offset=40000&limit=20 is easy to read, but the database may still skip 40,000 rows. A cursor can say “return the 20 entries after ID 9f3c.” An index can jump to that point, and new items are less likely to make the list skip or repeat entries.
steps.callout: Return the cursor for the next page. The app sends it back in its next request.

steps.title: Keep old apps working
body: A code cleanup renames name to display_name. The new app works, but many phones still use an older version and their profile screens now fail. You cannot force every phone to update. Evolve APIs by adding the new field and keeping the old one until it is no longer used. For a breaking change, publish a new version such as /v2/ and run both versions.
steps.callout: Every public API field is a promise. Measure which clients still use a field before removing or renaming it.

steps.title: Choose the API style
body:
Best forWatch out
RESTPublic APIs, simple read, create, update, and delete operations; cachingMay need many calls per screen
GraphQLMany clients with different screensExpensive queries and caching
gRPCCalls between servicesBrowsers need a proxy
Systems can mix styles: use REST or GraphQL for client apps and gRPC between internal services.
steps.callout: Whichever style you use, add fields instead of changing or removing fields that existing clients may depend on.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• An API is an agreement between programs.
  • REST uses resources and HTTP verbs. It is simple and cacheable, but a screen may need several calls.
  • GraphQL lets clients request selected fields in one query; limit expensive queries.
  • gRPC provides fast, typed calls between services.
  • Use cursors for long lists and evolve APIs without breaking old clients.
